$comment: R16: every structural guard ships with a documented mutation proving it
fails against broken code. A grep guard that passes against a broken
codebase converts an unknown into a false assurance, which is worse than
having no guard — and this project has already shipped one `sed` control
that silently never matched.
`verified` entries record a mutation that was applied, observed to fail,
and reverted. `grandfathered` is the ratchet: guards that predate this
registry and have no recorded control. That list may shrink and must never
grow — `negative-controls.test.ts` fails on a new structural guard with no
entry.
To clear a grandfathered entry: apply the mutation, run the suite, confirm
the guard fails, revert, and move it into `verified` with what you saw.
Never `git checkout` the file to revert if you have uncommitted work in it;
copy it aside first. That mistake has already cost this project a block of
unsaved analysis.
Rows marked `source: transcribed-at-merge` had their control run on the
branch that introduced the guard and recorded in that commit message. They
could not be registered there because this file lives on #265. Transcribed
rather than re-run; re-running them is worth doing and is a tracked task.
One qualification on "behavioural tests need no entry", learned at E8. A
behavioural test CAN pass vacuously when the thing it asserts is invisible
through the client it uses: `geofence-clear.itest.ts` could not tell
`Prisma.DbNull` from `Prisma.JsonNull`, because both read back as JS `null`
— so it agreed a fence was cleared while `geofence IS NULL` was false. It
took a raw-SQL assertion to see the difference. The rule still holds for
which tests need a registry entry; it does not mean a behavioural test is
automatically non-vacuous, only that it usually fails on its own terms.

undefined-query-budget.test.ts.note: Rewritten when the count reached zero. The old entry guarded a shrinking budget; at zero, 'found nothing' is the pass condition, so a broken counter and a clean tree became indistinguishable — control (c) is what separates them, and it needed a synthetic fixture because there is no longer a real site to find. Scope later widened to `scripts` after the flag broke `scripts/seed-qa.ts` and failed CI's e2e job at the seed step while every other job stayed green — the scan had been `app` and `lib` only. One of the two seed sites would still have escaped it, because the object is built outside the Prisma call; the flag caught what the scanner structurally cannot, which is the argument for having both.

select-fragment-collision.test.ts.guards: No object spreads two select fragments (or a fragment plus an inline key) that claim the same key, and the allowlist cannot go stale
select-fragment-collision.test.ts.mutation: Three: (a) add an inline `venue: true` beside `...eventPermissionSelect` in lib/sponsor-actions.ts; (b) delete the `...curationSelect` spread from the one allowlisted file; (c) point the fragment-detector regex at a name that matches nothing

select-fragment-collision.test.ts.note: Written because the rule had bitten three times and `tsc` caught only two. TS objects with TS2783 when two spreads are structurally incompatible, which is luck: two fragments both selecting a relation with different nested columns are assignable to each other, so the overwrite is silent — and a relation is where it costs most. The live case this guards is latent rather than present: `eventPermissionSelect` and `fenceSelect` both claim `venue`, nothing spreads both yet, and CLAUDE.md records that a select missing `venue` silently denies a venue owner.

Fixed with a fixture the detector runs against. The scan also needed narrowing three times, each the same mistake — a rule about what is emitted, written as a search for a string that also appears in what is read: first `user_id` in the Prisma select that feeds `mine`, then `authUser.userId` in the call computing it. snake_case is a column, camelCase is the wire, and only a `userId:` key is forbidden.

baseline-resurrection.test.ts.guards: The baseline creates nothing that a later migration drops — so replaying the chain onto a deployed database cannot resurrect a removed object
baseline-resurrection.test.ts.mutation: Two: (a) restore the `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... event_check_ins_event_id_user_id_key` line in the baseline; (b) point the DROP INDEX detector at a token that matches nothing
baseline-resurrection.test.ts.observed: (a) 1 failing — 'creates nothing that a later migration drops'; (b) 1 failing — 'detects a resurrection when there is one'; 3 passing after each revert
baseline-resurrection.test.ts.note: Written after the bug was found live. The baseline sorts first by name, so on a fresh install it creates the index and `20260807_event_occurrences` drops it moments later — correct. On staging that migration was recorded months ago, so the baseline applies AFTER it and re-creates the unique it existed to remove, making a second-day check-in violate a constraint. Nothing errors and the deploy succeeds. Found only by replaying against a schema-only copy of staging; every check against an empty database was green. The guard also had to strip SQL comments, because the fix leaves a note naming the index and a raw-text scan flags the very comment that records the fix.

workflow-yaml.test.ts.guards: No GitHub workflow carries a duplicate mapping key, which GitHub rejects outright while permissive YAML loaders accept silently
workflow-yaml.test.ts.mutation: Insert a second `if:` under the `e2e` job, immediately before `runs-on:` — the exact shape that shipped
workflow-yaml.test.ts.observed: 1 failing — 'has no duplicate keys'; 3 passing after revert
workflow-yaml.test.ts.note: Written after shipping the bug. Two `if:` keys on one job made every run on the branch invalid: the run is created, no job matches, and it reports as a plain red failure with zero jobs — indistinguishable from a broken test, and no `pull_request` check fires at all. It survived three commits because the check I was using was `yaml.safe_load`, which keeps the last duplicate and reports the file as clean. The detector here is line-based on purpose: every YAML parser available to it is the permissive one whose behaviour caused the bug. The first attempt at this control was also invalid — the anchor did not match, so the mutation never applied and the guard looked weak when it was not.
